group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 77-year-old man arrived by private automobile in the early afternoon after two days of progressive breathlessness that culminated in an early-morning episode in which he found himself gasping for air while seated at the kitchen table sipping coffee. He described the illness as beginning with mild chills, a dry cough, and low-grade fever the previous evening; overnight the cough became productive of tan sputum and he awoke drenched in perspiration, feeling “winded just standing up.” His spouse checked an oral temperature of 100.6 °F and, noting labored respirations, insisted on transport to the emergency department before any over-the-counter medications were taken. The patient lives in a single-story house, performs his own activities of daily living, and had walked the quarter-mile to the neighborhood mailbox without difficulty four days earlier; he has never required institutional care. His medical background is notable for long-standing systolic dysfunction with a most recent outpatient echocardiogram six months ago reporting an ejection fraction of 35 % and mild concentric hypertrophy. Nephrology follows him for Stage 4 chronic kidney disease related to decades of hypertensive nephrosclerosis; baseline serum creatinine last month measured 2.6 mg/dL and he has not yet required renal replacement therapy. He also carries a diagnosis of anemia of chronic disease for which no transfusions have been necessary, with a baseline hematocrit in the mid-20s. He denies prior transient ischemic attacks or cerebrovascular accidents, has no chronic liver disorder, and has never been treated for malignancy. Medications taken routinely include carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 24-26 mg twice daily, oral furosemide 40 mg each morning, amlodipine 5 mg nightly, and low-dose aspirin; he had ingested only his usual morning pills and half a cup of oatmeal before leaving home today. He quit smoking 25 years ago after a 20-pack-year exposure, drinks one glass of wine at holiday gatherings, and denies illicit drug use. Immunizations are current, including the seasonal influenza vaccine administered at a grocery-store clinic six weeks earlier and both pneumococcal injections within the past three years. Emergency medical services were not activated, and no supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, or antipyretics were given en route. In triage he sat leaning forward with elbows on his knees, speaking in short phrases yet fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Untreated vital signs documented temperature 38.1 °C, heart rate 105 beats per minute and regular, non-invasive blood pressure 109/66 mm Hg (systolic confirmed manually), respiratory rate 48 breaths per minute with visible alae nasi flaring, and pulse oximetry 86 % on ambient air at sea-level altitude. Skin was warm and lightly diaphoretic; mucous membranes were tacky. Jugular venous pulsation rose approximately 4 cm above the sternal angle, similar to cardiology notes. Cardiac auscultation revealed a rapid S1 and S2 with a soft third sound, no new murmurs, and no pericardial rub. Pulmonary examination showed coarse inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower and posterior mid-lung zones without dullness to percussion, and vesicular breath sounds elsewhere; no wheezes were heard. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender with normal bowel sounds; the liver edge was not palpable and there was no shifting dullness. Extremities were warm without cyanosis or edema, and capillary refill was brisk. A focused neurologic screen demonstrated equal, reactive pupils, intact cranial nerves, fluent speech, and full strength in all extremities. Finger-stick glucose prior to cannulation was 129 mg/dL. Venous blood samples and a right radial arterial puncture were obtained within ten minutes of arrival while the patient remained on room air. Basic metabolic panel returned sodium 119 mEq/L, potassium 4.9 mEq/L, chloride 93 mEq/L, bicarbonate 18 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 49 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, consistent with his chronic baseline trends except for the hyponatremia. Complete blood count revealed leukocytes 15.2 × 10⁹/L (88 % neutrophils), hematocrit 23 %, hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, and platelets 240 × 10⁹/L. An arterial blood gas obtained on ambient air showed pH 7.22, PaCO₂ 31 mm Hg, PaO₂ 54 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, indicating a primary metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation and significant hypoxemia. Serum lactate measured 2.6 mmol/L. A portable posteroanterior and lateral chest radiograph, performed before any therapy, demonstrated a dense right lower-lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, clear costophrenic angles, and a cardiothoracic ratio unchanged from prior imaging, with no evidence of fluid layering. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram captured concurrently showed sinus tachycardia at 106 beats per minute with nonspecific ST-T wave changes identical to outpatient tracings. Two sets of blood cultures, an expectorated sputum sample sent for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were collected prior to antibiotic administration. At the moment this note is completed the patient continues to breathe room air in a semi-upright position, has received no intravenous crystalloids, vasopressors, oxygen supplementation, diuretics, or antimicrobials beyond the small heparinized flush used for arterial sampling; thus all physiologic observations and laboratory data detailed above reflect his untreated baseline presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) adds demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points using admission findings.
- Demographics: for a man, start with age in years → 77. No nursing-home residence → 0.
- Comorbidities: systolic heart failure → 10; chronic renal disease → 10. No malignancy, liver disease, or cerebrovascular disease → 0 each.
- Examination: respiratory rate 48/min (≥30) → 20. He is oriented, SBP 109 mmHg is not <90, temperature 38.1°C is neither <35 nor ≥40, and pulse 105/min is not ≥125 → 0 each.
- Laboratory findings: arterial pH 7.22 (<7.35) → 30; BUN 49 mg/dL (≥30) → 20; sodium 119 mEq/L (<130) → 20; glucose 129 mg/dL (<250) → 0; hematocrit 23% (<30%) → 10.
- Oxygenation and imaging: room-air PaO₂ 54 mmHg (<60) → 10. SpO₂ 86% reflects the same hypoxemia and is not scored again. No pleural effusion → 0.
Total = 77 + 10 + 10 + 20 + 30 + 20 + 20 + 10 + 10 = 207 (class V).
Final answer: 207
